title: Go Error Semantics Across Service Boundaries: Typed Errors, Sentinel Values, and the gRPC Status Translation Problem
description: How Go error design degrades at service boundaries, and a production pattern for type-safe, observable error propagation across gRPC microservices.
linkedin_post:
Error handling in Go is clean inside a package. It degrades fast at a service boundary.

In a gRPC microservice graph, the default behavior is: your domain error hits the framework, gets serialized as codes.Unknown with a string message, and arrives at the caller with no structural identity. The caller can't use errors.Is or errors.As. It can't distinguish a validation rejection from a database timeout. It retries things it shouldn't and drops things it should retry.

I wrote up the mechanics of this problem and a production pattern for fixing it — typed DomainErrors with proto-serialized details, a translation layer at the server and client boundary, and observability emitted exactly at the seam where it's most meaningful.

The key decisions:
→ Domain errors carry a stable machine-readable Code field, not just a gRPC status code
→ The translation layer is the only place errors.As touches gRPC types
→ The shared package contains wire types and translation logic only — no service-specific imports
→ Callers branch on Code strings defined in the proto schema, not on parsing message text

This pattern adds about 80 lines of boilerplate. What it buys: callers that can make correct retry decisions, on-call engineers who can read a single trace span and know whose fault a failure was, and an error API that survives API versioning.

The decision framework at the end of the article is worth reading if you're evaluating whether this complexity is justified for your service graph.
